heading_en: To make a sect or a republic live long, it must often be drawn back toward its beginning
thesis: Mixed bodies such as republics, sects and kingdoms endure only if they are frequently renewed by being brought back toward their original principles, either by external shock, by internal laws and executions, or by the example of rare virtuous men.
thesis_quote: quelle sono meglio ordinate, ed hanno più lunga vita, che mediante gli ordini suoi si possono spesso rinnovare

propositions.statement: Mixed bodies that are not renewed toward their beginnings do not last, because the original goodness in them corrupts over time.
propositions.quote: Ed è cosa più chiara che la luce, che, non si rinnovando, questi corpi non durano.

propositions.statement: The return of a republic toward its beginning occurs either through external accident or through internal prudence (a law or a good man).
propositions.quote: Questa riduzione verso il principio, parlando delle republiche, si fa o per accidente estrinseco o per prudenza intrinseca

propositions.statement: No more than ten years should pass between notable executions, or men begin to alter their habits and transgress the laws.
propositions.quote: Perché dall’una all’altra di simili esecuzioni non vorrebbe passare, il più, dieci anni

propositions.statement: Renewal by external force, though sometimes an excellent remedy as at Rome, is so dangerous that it is in no way to be desired.
propositions.quote: ella è tanto pericolosa, che non è in modo alcuno da disiderarla

episodes.description: The capture of Rome by the Gauls forced the city to be reborn, retake religion and justice (neglected when the Fabii who fought contra ius gentium went unpunished and were made tribunes), and restore Camillus to authority.
episodes.quote: egli era necessario che Roma fussi presa dai Franciosi, a volere che la rinascesse

episodes.description: A series of notable executions pulled Rome back toward its principles: the death of Brutus's sons, of the Decemvirs, of Maelius the grain-dealer, of Manlius Capitolinus, of Manlius Torquatus's son, Papirius Cursor's proceeding against his master of horse Fabius, and the accusation of the Scipios.
episodes.quote: la morte de’ figliuoli di Bruto, la morte de’ dieci cittadini, quella di Melio frumentario

episodes.description: Rare virtuous individuals such as Horatius Cocles, Scaevola, Fabricius, the two Decii and Regulus Attilius produced in Rome almost the same effect as laws and orders through their examples.
episodes.quote: furono Orazio Cocle, Scevola, Fabrizio, i dua Deci, Regolo Attilio, ed alcuni altri

episodes.description: Those who governed Florence from 1434 to 1494 said it was necessary to retake the state every five years, renewing the terror and fear instilled when they first seized it.
episodes.quote: egli era necessario ripigliare ogni cinque anni lo stato, altrimenti, era difficile mantenerlo

episodes.description: Saint Francis and Saint Dominic renewed the Christian religion by poverty and the example of Christ's life, without which it would have been wholly extinguished.
episodes.quote: se non fossi stata ritirata verso il suo principio da Santo Francesco e da Santo Domenico sarebbe al tutto spenta

episodes.description: The kingdom of France is kept living under its laws by the parlements, above all that of Paris, which renew them by executions against princes of the realm and even condemn the king in its sentences.
episodes.quote: Delle quali leggi ed ordini ne sono mantenitori i parlamenti, e massime quel di Parigi

notes: Opening chapter of Book 3; Machiavelli announces the book's theme (how actions of particular men made Rome great). Doctors' maxim quoted in Latin is medical, not Livy.

heading_en: It is a very wise thing to simulate madness at the right time
thesis: A man of quality discontented with a prince must either openly make war on him if strong enough, or attach himself closely and feign compliance and even folly like Junius Brutus, since the middle way between closeness and distance is impossible.
thesis_quote: conviene ridursi a’ duoi modi soprascritti, cioè o di allargarsi o di stringersi con loro

propositions.statement: The middle course of being neither too near nor too far from a prince would be the truest if it could be observed, but it is impossible.
propositions.quote: la quale via del mezzo sarebbe la più vera, quando si potesse osservare; ma perché io credo che sia impossibile

propositions.statement: Notable men cannot choose to stand aside, for their excuses are heard but not accepted and they are not left alone.
propositions.quote: né possono gli uomini che hanno qualità, eleggere lo starsi, quando bene lo eleggessono veramente e sanza alcuna ambizione, perché non è loro creduto

propositions.statement: One must therefore play the madman like Brutus, praising, speaking and acting against one's own mind to please the prince.
propositions.quote: Conviene adunque fare il pazzo, come Bruto; ed assai si fa il matto, laudando, parlando, veggendo, faccendo cose contro allo animo tuo

episodes.description: Junius Brutus simulated stupidity to live safely under the Tarquins and awaited his occasion, showing his design when he interpreted Apollo's oracle by pretending to fall and kiss the earth.
episodes.quote: si vide, prima, nello interpetrare l’oracolo d’Apolline, quando simulò cadere per baciare la terra

episodes.description: Over the dead Lucretia, Brutus was the first to draw the knife from her wound and made the bystanders swear never to allow anyone to reign in Rome again.
episodes.quote: ei fu il primo a trarle il coltello della ferita, e fare giurare ai circustanti

notes: Machiavelli notes Livy gives only one motive (safety of life and patrimony) and infers the political motive himself.

heading_en: To maintain a newly acquired liberty it is necessary to kill the sons of Brutus
thesis: After a change of state, a memorable execution against the enemies of the new order is necessary: whoever makes a free state and does not kill the sons of Brutus, like Piero Soderini, maintains himself only a short time.
thesis_quote: chi piglia una tirannide e non ammazza Bruto, e chi fa uno stato libero e non ammazza i figliuoli di Bruto, si mantiene poco tempo

propositions.statement: After any mutation of state, from republic to tyranny or tyranny to republic, a memorable execution against the enemies of the present conditions is necessary.
propositions.quote: dopo una mutazione di stato, o da republica in tirannide o da tirannide in republica è necessaria una esecuzione memorabile contro a’ nimici delle condizioni presenti

propositions.statement: One must never let an evil run on out of regard for a good, when that good can easily be crushed by that evil.
propositions.quote: e’ non si debbe mai lasciare scorrere un male, rispetto ad uno bene, quando quel bene facilmente possa essere, da quel male, oppressato

propositions.statement: Malignity is neither tamed by time nor placated by any gift.
propositions.quote: la malignità non è doma da tempo né placata da alcuno dono

episodes.description: Brutus sat in judgment and not only condemned his own sons to death for conspiring against the new liberty but was present at their execution.
episodes.quote: vedere il padre sedere pro tribunali, e non solamente condennare i suoi figliuoli a morte ma essere presente alla morte loro

episodes.description: Piero Soderini believed he could overcome with patience and goodness the appetite of the 'sons of Brutus' to return to another government, refused to seize extraordinary authority to crush them, and lost his position, his reputation and his country.
episodes.quote: il quale si credeva superare con la pazienza e bontà sua quello appetito che era ne’ figliuoli di Bruto

heading_en: A prince does not live secure in a principality while those despoiled of it are alive
thesis: A prince who has stripped others of a kingdom is never safe while they live, for old injuries are never cancelled by new benefits, as the deaths of Tarquinius Priscus and Servius Tullius show.
thesis_quote: si può avvertire ogni principe, che non viva mai sicuro del suo principato, finché vivono coloro che ne sono stati spogliati

propositions.statement: Old injuries are never cancelled by new benefits, the less so the smaller the new benefit is relative to the injury.
propositions.quote: mai le ingiurie vecchie furono cancellate da’ beneficii nuovi; e, tanto meno, quanto il beneficio nuovo è minore che non è stata la ingiuria

propositions.statement: The appetite for reigning is so great that it enters not only the breasts of those who expect the kingdom but also of those who do not.
propositions.quote: questo appitito del regnare è tanto grande, che non solamente entra ne’ petti di coloro a chi si aspetta il regno, ma di quelli a chi e’ non si aspetta

episodes.description: Tarquinius Priscus, believing he possessed the kingdom juridically by gift of the people and Senate, was killed by the sons of Ancus whom he had despoiled of it.
episodes.quote: La morte di Tarquinio Prisco causata dai figliuoli di Anco

episodes.description: Servius Tullius, who thought he could win over the sons of Tarquin with new merits, was killed by Tarquinius Superbus, urged on by Servius's own daughter Tullia, who valued being queen more than being a king's daughter.
episodes.quote: la morte di Servio Tullo causata da Tarquinio Superbo

heading_en: What makes a king who inherits a kingdom lose it
thesis: Hereditary kings begin to lose their state the moment they break the ancient laws and customs under which men have long lived: Tarquin the Proud was expelled for governing tyrannically, not because of the rape of Lucretia.
thesis_quote: a quella ora ei cominciano a perdere lo stato che cominciano a rompere le leggi, e quelli modi e quelle consuetudini che sono antiche

propositions.statement: Tarquin was expelled not because his son Sextus raped Lucretia, but because he broke the laws of the kingdom and governed it tyrannically.
propositions.quote: Non fu, adunque, cacciato costui per avere Sesto suo figliuolo stuprata Lucrezia, ma per avere rotte le leggi del regno, e governatolo tirannicamente

propositions.statement: Had Tarquin lived like the other kings, Brutus and Collatinus would have appealed to Tarquin himself for vengeance against Sextus, not to the Roman people.
propositions.quote: Perché se Tarquinio fosse vissuto come gli altri re, e Sesto suo figliuolo avessi fatto quello errore, sarebbono Bruto e Collatino ricorsi a Tarquinio

propositions.statement: Men who are well governed neither seek nor want any further liberty.
propositions.quote: gli uomini, quando sono governati bene, non cercono né vogliono altra libertà

episodes.description: Tarquinius Superbus stripped the Senate of all authority, drew public business into his own palace, and wore out the plebs in menial works, filling Rome with cruel and proud examples that disposed all Romans to rebellion.
episodes.quote: avendo tolto al Senato ogni autorità, e ridottola a sé proprio

episodes.description: The incident of Lucretia was only the occasion of Tarquin's expulsion; had it not come, another accident would soon have produced the same effect.
episodes.quote: E, se lo accidente di Lucrezia non fosse venuto, come prima ne fosse nato un altro, arebbe partorito il medesimo effetto

episodes.description: Timoleon of Corinth and Aratus of Sicyon governed so well that their peoples constrained them to remain princes for life although they repeatedly tried to return to private life.
episodes.quote: come sarebbe Timoleone Corintio, Arato Sicioneo, e simili

thesis: Conspiracies have cost more princes their lives and states than open war, yet are supremely dangerous to the conspirators at every stage (planning, execution, aftermath); princes should learn to guard against them, above all against universal hatred, and private men to abstain from them.
thesis_quote: si vede per quelle molti più principi avere perduta la vita e lo stato, che per guerra aperta

propositions.statement: The most important cause of conspiracy against a prince is being hated by the generality, which gives injured individuals both the desire for revenge and encouragement from the universal ill-disposition.
propositions.quote: E questa è lo essere odiato dallo universale, perché il principe che si è concitato questo universale odio, è ragionevole che abbi de’ particulari i quali da lui siano stati più offesi

propositions.statement: In injuries of blood, threats are far more dangerous than executions: the dead cannot think of revenge, but a man threatened is forced either to act or to suffer.
propositions.quote: Di quelle del sangue sono più pericolose le minacce che le esecuzioni; anzi, le minacce sono pericolosissime, e nelle esecuzioni non vi è pericolo alcuno

propositions.statement: A prince who would guard himself from conspiracies should fear those on whom he has heaped too many favors more than those he has injured too much, for the former have the means the latter lack.
propositions.quote: Debbe, adunque, uno principe che si vuole guardare dalle congiure, temere più coloro a chi elli ha fatto troppi piaceri, che quelli a chi egli avesse fatte troppe ingiurie

propositions.statement: The one true remedy against discovery is to give conspirators no time to accuse you: communicate the affair only at the moment of execution, never before.
propositions.quote: Il primo ed il più vero, anzi, a dire meglio, unico, è non dare tempo ai congiurati di accusarti; e comunicare loro la cosa quando tu la vuoi fare, e non prima

episodes.description: Pausanias, a noble known to the prince, killed Philip of Macedon on his way to the temple though surrounded by a thousand armed men, between his son and his son-in-law.
episodes.quote: Pausania, del quale altre volte si è parlato, ammazzò Filippo di Macedonia che andava al tempio, con mille armati d’intorno

episodes.description: A poor and abject Spaniard stabbed King Ferdinand of Spain in the neck; the wound was not mortal, but it showed that such a man had the spirit and the opportunity.
actors: Ferdinand of Aragon, king of Spain
episodes.quote: Uno spagnuolo, povero ed abietto, dette una coltellata in su el collo al re Ferrando, re di Spagna

episodes.description: A dervish, a Turkish priest, drew a scimitar against Bajazet, father of the present Turk; he did not wound him but had the spirit and opportunity to attempt it.
episodes.quote: Uno dervis, sacerdote turchesco, trasse d’una scimitarra a Baisit, padre del presente Turco

episodes.description: Lucio Belanti conspired against Pandolfo Petrucci, tyrant of Siena, for having given and then taken back his daughter as wife; the ambush at his house failed when a friend stopped Pandolfo just before the signal, and Belanti and his companions had to flee Siena.
episodes.quote: Luzio Belanti non si mosse a congiurare contro a Pandolfo tiranno di Siena, se non per averli quello data e poi tolta per moglie una sua figliuola

episodes.description: The Pazzi conspired against Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, moved above all by the Bonromei inheritance taken from them; over fifty accomplices kept the secret until the execution, but the sudden change of plan to the cathedral, Montesecco's refusal to kill in church, and Antonio da Volterra's shout 'Ah traditore!' ruined it, and only Giuliano was killed.
episodes.quote: La congiura de’ Pazzi contro a Lorenzo e Giuliano de’ Medici, è nota

episodes.description: The desire to free the fatherland moved Brutus and Cassius against Caesar; on the morning of the deed a long talk between Caesar and the conspirator Popilius Laenas nearly made them strike prematurely, and because the people loved Caesar they later avenged him, hunting down all the conspirators.
episodes.quote: Questa cagione mosse Bruto e Cassio contro a Cesare

episodes.description: Perennius against Commodus, Plautianus against Severus and Sejanus against Tiberius all conspired out of excess of benefits, raised so high that only the empire seemed lacking, and all ended as their ingratitude deserved.
episodes.quote: come fu Perennio contro a Commodo, Plauziano contro a Severo, Seiano contro a Tiberio

episodes.description: Iacopo d'Appiano, raised and made reputable by Piero Gambacorti, prince of Pisa, then took his state from him — a conspiracy of a beneficiary that succeeded.
episodes.quote: quella di Iacopo di Appiano contro a messer Piero Gambacorti, principe di Pisa

episodes.description: Coppola, risen so high under King Ferdinand of Aragon that only the kingdom seemed lacking to him, lost his life wanting that too.
actors: Ferdinand I of Aragon, king of Naples
episodes.quote: Fu di queste quella del Coppola, ne’ nostri tempi, contro il re Ferrando d’Aragona

episodes.description: The Pisonian conspiracy against Nero was betrayed by conjecture: the day before the deed Scaevinus made his will, had his freedman Milichius sharpen an old dagger, freed his slaves and prepared bandages, and Milichius accused him; Scaevinus and Natalis contradicted each other and the conspiracy was destroyed — though Piso, great and familiar with Nero, could have killed him in his own gardens.
episodes.quote: Scevino, uno de’ congiurati, il dì dinanzi ch’egli aveva ad ammazzare Nerone, fece testamento

episodes.description: Epicharis, once Nero's friend, told a captain of Nero's triremes of the conspiracy but not the conspirators' names; when he broke faith and accused her, her audacity in denying it left Nero confused and she was not condemned.
episodes.quote: fu tanta l’audacia di Epicari nel negarlo, che Nerone, rimaso confuso, non la condannò

episodes.description: The sons of Brutus, negotiating with the envoys of Tarquin, were overheard by a slave who accused them — discovery through lack of prudence.
episodes.quote: come intervenne ai figliuoli di Bruto, che, nel maneggiare la cosa con i legati di Tarquinio, furono intesi da uno servo

episodes.description: Dymnus, one of the conspirators with Philotas against Alexander the Great, told the plot to Nicomachus, a boy he loved, who told his brother Ciballinus, who told the king.
episodes.quote: come fece Dimmo, uno de’ congiurati con Filota contro a Alessandro Magno

episodes.description: In the conspiracy against Hieronymus, king of Syracuse, the captured conspirator Theodorus concealed all his fellows and accused the king's friends instead, while the conspirators trusted his virtue so fully that none fled or showed fear.
episodes.quote: nella congiura fatta contro a Girolamo, re di Siracusa; dove, sendo Teodoro, uno de’ congiurati, preso

episodes.description: Nelematus, unable to bear the tyranny of Aristotimus of Epirus, gathered kinsmen and friends in his house, locked the doors, and forced them to swear to act at once or be handed over to the tyrant; the execution succeeded immediately.
episodes.quote: Nelemato, non potendo sopportare la tirannide di Aristotimo, tiranno di Epiro, ragunò in casa sua molti parenti ed amici

episodes.description: When a Magus had seized the kingdom of Persia by fraud, Ortanes revealed it to six princes, and Darius forced immediate action with the threat of denouncing them all, whereupon they executed their design successfully without giving anyone time to repent.
episodes.quote: Avendo uno Mago, per inganno, occupato il regno de’ Persi

episodes.description: The Aetolians sent Alexamenus with thirty horse and two hundred foot to Nabis, tyrant of Sparta, under color of aid, imposing blind obedience on the others and confiding the secret to Alexamenus alone, who revealed it only at the moment of execution and succeeded in killing Nabis.
episodes.quote: i quali mandarono Alessameno loro cittadino, con trenta cavagli e dugento fanti, a Nabide, sotto colore di mandargli aiuto

episodes.description: Plautianus charged the tribune Saturninus with killing the emperor Severus and his son Antoninus; Saturninus demanded a written warrant, which Plautianus, blinded by ambition, gave him, and by that note Plautianus was accused and convicted.
episodes.quote: Plauziano, volendo fare ammazzare Severo imperadore ed Antonino suo figliuolo, commisse la cosa a Saturnino tribuno

episodes.description: Commodus listed Marcia, Laetus and Eclectus for death; a favorite boy carried the list out of the bedroom, Marcia read it, and the three, knowing the necessity, killed Commodus that very night — strangling him when the poison was thrown up.
episodes.quote: conosciuto tutti a tre il pericolo in quale erano, deliberorono prevenire; e, sanza mettere tempo in mezzo, la notte sequente ammazzorono Commodo

episodes.description: Antoninus Caracalla wrote from Mesopotamia to have the astrologers name who aspired to the empire; Maternianus's reply naming the prefect Macrinus reached Macrinus first, who, facing the necessity of killing or dying, had the centurion Martial (whose brother Antoninus had killed) slay him.
episodes.quote: commisse a Marziale centurione, suo fidato, ed a chi Antonino aveva morto, pochi giorni innanzi uno fratello, che lo ammazzasse

episodes.description: A slave sent to kill Marius, prisoner of the people of Minturnae, was so terrified by his presence and the memory of his name that he lost all strength to kill him — the majesty of a great man cows an executioner.
episodes.quote: A Mario, essendo preso da’ Minturnesi, fu mandato uno servo che lo ammazzasse

episodes.description: Conspirators against Sitalces, king of Thrace, repeatedly met at the appointed place and time but none dared strike; discovered, they bore the penalty for the evil they could have done but would not.
episodes.quote: Congiurorono alcuni contro a Sitalce re di Tracia, deputorono il dì della esecuzione

episodes.description: Two brothers of Alfonso, duke of Ferrara, conspired against him using the priest-singer Giannes as go-between, who several times brought the duke among them, yet none ever dared kill him; discovered, they paid the penalty of their wickedness and imprudence.
actors: Alfonso I d'Este, duke of Ferrara
episodes.quote: Congiurarono contro a Alfonso, duca di Ferrara, due sui frategli, ed usarono mezzano Giannes, prete e cantore del duca

episodes.description: Lucilla, sister of Commodus, arranged for Quintianus to kill him; waiting at the amphitheater entrance with a naked dagger he cried 'This the Senate sends you!' and was seized before his arm fell.
episodes.quote: Lucilla, sirocchia di Commodo, ordinò che Quinziano lo ammazzassi

episodes.description: Athenian youths conspired against Diocles and Hippias, tyrants of Athens; they killed Diocles, but Hippias survived and avenged him.
episodes.quote: Congiurorono certi giovani ateniesi contro a Diocle ed Ippia, tiranni di Atene

episodes.description: Chion and Leonides of Heraclea, disciples of Plato, conspired against the tyrants Clearchus and Satyrus; they killed Clearchus, but Satyrus survived and avenged him.
episodes.quote: Chione e Leonide eraclensi e discepoli di Platone, congiurarono contro a Clearco e Satiro, tiranni

episodes.description: Pelopidas, though an exile without easy access, conspired against ten tyrants of Thebes and, with the help of Charon, a counselor of the tyrants, killed them and freed his fatherland — a success so rare that writers celebrate it as almost without example.
episodes.quote: la congiura che Pelopida fece per liberare Tebe sua patria, ebbe tutte le difficultà: nondimeno ebbe felicissimo fine

episodes.description: Giovanni Andrea da Lampognano and his fellow conspirators killed the duke of Milan, but a son and two brothers of the duke remained in time to avenge him.
actors: Galeazzo Maria Sforza, duke of Milan
episodes.quote: come intervenne a Giovanni Andrea da Lampognano, il quale, insieme con i suoi congiurati, avendo morto il duca di Milano

episodes.description: Conspirators of Forlì killed Count Girolamo and held his wife and small children, but let Countess Caterina enter the fortress on her promise to surrender it; from the walls she threatened them with every revenge, showing her genitals to prove she could make more children, and they ended in perpetual exile.
episodes.quote: Ammazzarono alcuni congiurati Forlivesi il conte Girolamo loro signore, presono la moglie, ed i suoi figliuoli

episodes.description: Catiline, his conspiracy against the fatherland discovered, not only remained in Rome but came to the Senate and insulted it and the consul; Lentulus and the others were seized only because letters in their own hand manifestly accused them.
episodes.quote: Ciascuno ha letto la congiura di Catilina scritta da Sallustio

episodes.description: Hanno of Carthage, aspiring to tyranny, planned to poison the whole Senate at his daughter's wedding; the Senate, learning of it, only passed a law limiting banquet expenses; he then armed many thousands of partisans and was killed with them.
episodes.quote: Annone, grandissimo cittadino in Cartagine, aspirando alla tirannide, aveva ordinato nelle nozze d’una sua figliuola di avvelenare tutto il Senato

episodes.description: Pisistratus of Athens, having beaten the Megarians and gained favor with the people, came out one morning wounded, claimed the nobility had injured him out of envy, obtained an armed guard, and from that authority rose to tyranny.
episodes.quote: avendo Pisistrato ateniese vinti i Megarensi, e per questo acquistata grazia nel popolo, uscì una mattina fuora, ferito

episodes.description: Pandolfo Petrucci returned to Siena with other exiles and was given the guard of the piazza as a menial charge others refused; those armed men in time gave him such reputation that he shortly became prince.
episodes.quote: Pandolfo Petrucci tornò, con altri fuora usciti, in Siena, e gli fu data la guardia della piazza

episodes.description: Some leading citizens of Thebes called in a Spartan army to help them make themselves tyrants, and seized the tyranny of that city with foreign forces.
episodes.quote: Alcuni primi cittadini di Tebe per farsi tiranni chiamorono in aiuto uno esercito spartano, e presono la tirannide di quella città

episodes.description: The heads of the two Roman legions left to guard the Capuans against the Samnites conspired to oppress the Capuans; Rome sent the new consul Rutilius, who lulled them by announcing their quarters were confirmed, and only when he began separating them did they take alarm, reveal themselves and act.
episodes.quote: congiurarono quelli capi delle legioni insieme di opprimere i Capovani

episodes.description: The duke of Athens, become tyrant of Florence, on learning of a conspiracy had one conspirator seized without weighing the conspirators' forces, whereupon the others immediately took arms and took the state from him; he had also earlier put to death a man who revealed a conspiracy to him.
actors: Walter of Brienne, duke of Athens
episodes.quote: Il duca, diventato tiranno di Firenze, ed intendendo esserli congiurato contro, fece, sanza esaminare altrimenti la cosa, pigliare uno de’ congiurati

episodes.description: Guglielmo de' Pazzi, commissioner in Val di Chiana in 1501, hearing of a conspiracy in Arezzo in favor of the Vitelli, had one conspirator seized without preparing any force; the others took arms, took the town from the Florentines, and made Guglielmo a prisoner.
episodes.quote: Guglielmo, sendo commessario in Val di Chiana nel 1501, ed avendo inteso come in Arezzo era una congiura in favore de’ Vitelli

episodes.description: Dion of Syracuse, to test a suspect, let his trusted Callippus pretend to conspire against him; Callippus, able to practice against Dion without fear, conspired in earnest and took from him his state and his life.
episodes.quote: Dione siragusano, il quale, per tentare l’animo di alcuno che elli aveva a sospetto, consentì a Callippo, nel quale ei confidava

notes: Longest chapter of the Discorsi. Livy is explicitly cited for the Hieronymus of Syracuse conspiracy (Livy XXIV, outside I-X) and for the Latin quote on Alexamenus ('Collegit et ipse animum...', Livy XXXV); hence no I-X candidates for those. Most examples are post-Livian, Greek, or contemporary.

heading_en: Why some changes between liberty and servitude are bloodless and others full of blood
thesis: Whether a change of state is bloody depends on whether the state being changed was born in violence: states born with the injury of many provoke vengeance at their fall, while states founded on common consent harm only their head when they collapse.
thesis_quote: Il che depende da questo: perché quello stato che si muta, nacque con violenza, o no

propositions.statement: A state born with violence is born with injury to many, and at its ruin the injured seek revenge, whence come blood and the death of men.
propositions.quote: quando e’ nasce con violenza, conviene nasca con ingiuria di molti, è necessario poi, nella rovina sua, che gl’ingiuriati si voglino vendicare

propositions.statement: A state created by the common consent of a universality that made it great has, when it falls, no cause to offend anyone but its head.
propositions.quote: quando quello stato è causato da uno comune consenso d’una universalità che lo ha fatto grande, non ha cagione poi, quando rovina detta universalità, di offendere altri che il capo

episodes.description: In the change Rome made from kings to consuls, no one was driven out or harmed except the Tarquins, because the royal state had rested on common consent.
episodes.quote: come intervenne nella mutazione che fe’ Roma dai Re a’ Consoli, dove non furono cacciati altri che i Tarquinii

episodes.description: At the fall of the Medici state in Florence in 1494, no one was harmed except the Medici themselves.
episodes.quote: come fu ancora in Firenze lo stato de’ Medici, che poi nelle rovine loro, nel 1494, non furono offesi altri che loro

heading_en: He who would alter a republic must consider its subject matter
thesis: A wicked citizen can do no harm in an uncorrupted republic; whoever would seize authority and impose a bad form must find the matter already disordered by time, and in all great actions men must suit themselves to the times.
thesis_quote: uno tristo cittadino non può male operare in una republica che non sia corrotta

propositions.statement: To seize authority in a republic and impose a bad form, one must find the matter disordered by time, brought little by little, generation by generation, to disorder.
propositions.quote: Però è bisogno, a volere pigliare autorità in una republica e mettervi trista forma, trovare la materia disordinata dal tempo

propositions.statement: One man's life cannot suffice to corrupt a republic so that he himself can draw the fruit of it.
propositions.quote: gli è impossibile che la vita d’uno basti a corromperla in modo che egli medesimo ne possa trarre frutto

propositions.statement: Had Manlius been born in the corrupt times of Marius and Sulla he would have had their successes, and had they been born in his times they would have been crushed at their first enterprises.
propositions.quote: se Manlio fusse nato ne’ tempi di Mario e di Silla, dove già la materia era corrotta e dove esso arebbe potuto imprimere la forma dell’ambizione sua, arebbe avuti quegli medesimi séguiti e successi che Mario e Silla

propositions.statement: It is as difficult and dangerous to free a people that wants to live servile as to enslave a people that wants to live free.
propositions.quote: tanto è difficile e pericoloso volere fare libero uno popolo che voglia vivere servo, quanto è volere fare servo uno popolo che voglia vivere libero

episodes.description: Spurius Cassius, ambitious to win the plebs with benefits like dividing the lands taken from the Hernici, was suspected by the Fathers, and when he offered the people the money from the Sicilian grain they refused it outright as the price of their liberty.
episodes.quote: offerendo di darli quelli danari che si erano ritratti dei grani che il publico aveva fatti venire di Sicilia, al tutto gli recusò

episodes.description: Manlius Capitolinus, out of envy of Camillus's honors, stirred tumults against the Senate and the laws; neither nobility, kin nor tribunes defended him, and the people, made judge of his cause, condemned him to death without regard to his past merits.
episodes.quote: si misse a fare tumulti in Roma contro al Senato e contro alle leggi patrie

notes: Livy quoted verbatim: 'Hunc exitum habuit vir, nisi in libera civitate natus esset, memorabilis' (Livy 6.20).

heading_en: One must vary with the times in order always to have good fortune
thesis: Good and bad fortune come from matching one's mode of proceeding with the times; since men cannot change their nature or abandon ways that have prospered, fortune varies for individuals, and republics outlive principalities because their diverse citizens suit diverse times.
thesis_quote: la cagione della trista e della buona fortuna degli uomini è riscontrare il modo del procedere suo con i tempi

propositions.statement: He errs least and has prosperous fortune who matches his mode of proceeding with the time, while always proceeding as nature compels.
propositions.quote: Ma quello viene ad errare meno, ed avere la fortuna prospera, che riscontra, come ho detto, con il suo modo il tempo

propositions.statement: A republic has longer life and better fortune than a principality because the diversity of its citizens lets it accommodate itself to the diversity of the times.
propositions.quote: una republica ha maggiore vita, ed ha più lungamente buona fortuna, che uno principato; perché la può meglio accomodarsi alla diversità de’ temporali, per la diversità de’ cittadini

propositions.statement: Men cannot change their modes both because they cannot oppose their natural inclination and because, having prospered one way, they cannot be persuaded to proceed otherwise.
propositions.quote: l’una, che noi non ci possiamo opporre a quello a che c'inclina la natura; l’altra, che, avendo uno con uno modo di procedere prosperato assai, non è possibile persuadergli che possa fare bene a procedere altrimenti

episodes.description: Fabius Maximus's natural caution and delay matched the times when Hannibal, young and in fresh fortune, had twice beaten Rome; but Fabius later opposed Scipio's crossing to Africa because he could not depart from his ways, while the republic could turn to Scipio when the times suited winning the war.
episodes.quote: Ciascuno sa come Fabio Massimo procedeva con lo esercito suo rispettivamente e cautamente, discosto da ogni impeto e da ogni audacia romana

episodes.description: Piero Soderini proceeded in all things with humanity and patience and prospered while the times conformed, but when times came that required breaking with patience and humility he could not do it, and fell together with his country.
episodes.quote: Piero Soderini, altre volte preallegato, procedeva in tutte le cose sue con umanità e pazienza

episodes.description: Pope Julius II proceeded throughout his pontificate with impetus and fury, and because the times accompanied him all his enterprises succeeded; had other times come he would necessarily have fallen.
episodes.quote: Papa Iulio II procedette in tutto il tempo del suo pontificato con impeto e con furia

notes: Parallel to Il Principe ch. 25 on fortune and the times.

heading_en: A captain cannot avoid battle when the adversary wants it at any cost
thesis: A captain who keeps the field cannot avoid battle when the enemy insists on it at any cost; commissions to avoid battle above all things are null or harmful, for the only alternatives — keeping fifty miles away or shutting oneself in a city — are ruinous.
thesis_quote: uno capitano, che voglia stare alla campagna, non può fuggire la giornata, qualunque volta il nemico la vuole fare in ogni modo

propositions.statement: The commission given to captains to avoid battle above all things is most of the time null or harmful.
propositions.quote: non intendono che, la maggiore parte delle volte, questa commissione è nulla o è dannosa

propositions.statement: To stay in the field without battle there is no safe remedy but to keep at least fifty miles from the enemy with good spies; the other course, shutting into a city, means siege, hunger and surrender.
propositions.quote: non ci è altro rimedio sicuro che porsi cinquanta miglia almeno discosto al nimico

propositions.statement: A prince whose army must dissolve for lack of money or friends is utterly mad if he does not try fortune before it dissolves: waiting he loses for certain, trying he might win.
propositions.quote: è matto al tutto se non tenta la fortuna innanzi che tale esercito si abbia a risolvere: perché, aspettando e’ perde il certo; tentando, potrebbe vincere

propositions.statement: Even losing, one should want to acquire glory; and there is more glory in being beaten by force than by some other inconvenience that made you lose.
propositions.quote: si debbe, eziandio perdendo, volere acquistare gloria; e più gloria si ha, ad essere vinto per forza, che per altro inconveniente che ti abbi fatto perdere

episodes.description: The dictator Gnaeus Sulpicius drew out the war against the Gauls, unwilling to commit himself to fortune against an enemy whom time and an alien position made worse by the day.
episodes.quote: «Cneus Sulpitius dictator adversus Gallos bellum trahebat, nolens se fortunae committere adversus hostem, quem tempus deteriorem in dies, et locus alienus, faceret»

episodes.description: Philip of Macedon, father of Perseus, attacked by the Romans, first fortified a mountaintop like Fabius and was driven off it in battle, then kept his distance province by province, and finally, his condition worsening, resolved to try the fortune of a pitched battle.
episodes.quote: Filippo, sendo assaltato dai Romani, deliberò non venire alla zuffa; e, per non vi venire, volle fare prima come aveva fatto Fabio Massimo in Italia

episodes.description: Fabius Maximus stood in strong places with so good an army that Hannibal never dared seek him out there: the battle was avoided as much by Hannibal as by Fabius, not refused by Fabius.
episodes.quote: Il modo che tenne Fabio Massimo, di stare ne’ luoghi forti, è buono quando tu hai sì virtuoso esercito

episodes.description: Hannibal facing Scipio in Africa accepted battle; being a master of war he would have delayed had he seen advantage in it, so some weighty necessity must have moved him, while Scipio, having beaten Syphax and taken many towns, could stay in Africa in safety.
episodes.quote: ed essendo allo incontro di Scipione in Affrica, s’egli avessi veduto vantaggio in allungare la guerra, ei lo arebbe fatto

episodes.description: Duke Charles of Burgundy, encamped at Morat, a town of the Swiss, was assaulted and routed by the Swiss — the besieger cannot refuse battle.
actors: Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy
episodes.quote: intervenne al duca Carlo di Borgogna, che, sendo accampato a Moratto, terra de’ Svizzeri, fu da’ Svizzeri assaltato e rotto

episodes.description: The French army besieging Novara was likewise routed by the Swiss.
episodes.quote: come intervenne allo esercito di Francia, che, campeggiando Novara, fu medesimamente da’ Svizzeri rotto

notes: Chapter opens and closes with the same Latin quotation from Livy 7.12, explicitly attributed ('per le ragioni che dice Tito Livio').

heading_en: He who has to deal with many, though weaker, wins if he can withstand the first attacks
thesis: When many powers unite against one, the one will end superior if he has virtue enough to sustain the first assaults and temporize, for with a little industry the many can always be disunited.
thesis_quote: quello uno abbia a restare superiore, quando sia di tale virtù, che possa sostenere i primi impeti, e col temporeggiarsi aspettare tempo

propositions.statement: When many powerful men are united against one, one should always hope more in the single, less strong one than in the many, however strong.
propositions.quote: si debbe sempre sperare più in quel solo e men gagliardo che in quelli assai, ancora che gagliardissimi

propositions.statement: Using a little industry, the one can always disunite the many and weaken the body that was strong.
propositions.quote: potrà, usando un poco d’industria, disunire gli assai; e quel corpo, ch’era gagliardo, fare debole

episodes.description: Appius Claudius showed the nobility how to defend itself against the ambition of the tribunes: always find among them one who is fearful, corruptible or a lover of the common good, and dispose him to oppose the will of the others — a tempering that long benefited Rome.
episodes.quote: da Appio Claudio non fosse stato mostro il modo con il quale si avevano a difendere contro all’ambizione de’ Tribuni

episodes.description: In 1483 all Italy leagued against the Venetians; when they could no longer keep the field, they corrupted Lodovico who governed Milan and made an accord by which they recovered their lost towns and usurped part of the state of Ferrara, losing the war but winning the peace.
episodes.quote: Congiurò nel 1483 tutta Italia contro ai Viniziani

episodes.description: A few years ago the whole world leagued against France, yet before the end of the war Spain broke from the confederates and made its own accord, forcing the others soon to come to terms as well.
episodes.quote: Pochi anni sono, congiurò contro a Francia tutto il mondo: nondimeno, avanti che si vedesse il fine della guerra, Spagna si ribellò da’ confederati

episodes.description: The Venetians in 1508 lacked armies with which to temporize against the French and so had no time to detach any of the league; the Pope and Spain, once their own claims were recovered, would gladly have saved Lombardy for them against France.
episodes.quote: come intervenne a’ Viniziani nell’otto, i quali, se avessero potuto temporeggiare con lo esercito francioso

heading_en: A prudent captain must impose on his soldiers every necessity to fight, and take it from the enemy's
thesis: Necessity makes soldiers obstinate in combat; a prudent captain should therefore contrive to impose the necessity of fighting on his own men and to remove it from the enemy's, in sieges as in the field.
thesis_quote: facevano ogni opera perché i soldati loro fussero constretti da quella; e, dall’altra parte, usavono ogni industria perché gli nimici se ne liberassero

propositions.statement: A captain should measure the ease or difficulty of storming a town by the necessity that constrains its inhabitants to defend themselves.
propositions.quote: debbe misurare la facilità o la difficultà dello espugnarla, dal conoscere e considerare quale necessità constringa gli abitatori di quella a difendersi

propositions.statement: Towns are harder to take after rebellion than at first acquisition, because fearing punishment for their offense they become difficult to storm.
propositions.quote: le terre, dopo la rebellione, sono più difficili ad acquistare, che le non sono nel primo acquisto

propositions.statement: An attacking captain should strive to take from the defenders their necessity and hence their obstinacy, promising pardon and professing to act only against a few ambitious men.
propositions.quote: con ogni diligenza ingegnarsi di levare, a’ difensori di quella, tale necessità, e, per consequenzia, tale ostinazione; promettendo perdono

episodes.description: Florence, surrounded by free cities obstinate in their defense out of neighborly rivalry, has spent more in its wars and acquired less than Venice, whose neighboring towns, used to living under princes, often cared little about changing masters.
episodes.quote: Firenze abbia più speso nelle guerre, ed acquistato meno di Vinegia

episodes.description: Crassus's army, blinded by the Parthians' offers of peace made to remove his soldiers' necessity of defending themselves, could not be kept obstinate even though Crassus saw through the vain promises.
episodes.quote: come intervenne a Crasso ed allo esercito suo: il quale, come che conoscesse le vane promesse de’ Parti

episodes.description: The Samnites, their peace embassy rebuffed by Rome, were shown by their captain Claudius Pontius that war was now necessary — 'war is just for those to whom it is necessary' — and on that necessity he founded his soldiers' hope of victory.
episodes.quote: «Iustum est bellum quibus necessarium, et pia arma quibus nisi in armis spes est»

episodes.description: Gaius Manilius, facing the Veientes, blocked all exits of his camp when part of their army got inside the stockade; the enclosed Veientes fought with such rage that they killed Manilius, and only a tribune's prudence in opening them a way out saved the rest of the Romans.
episodes.quote: perché i Veienti non potessino salvarsi, occupò tutti gli aditi del campo; donde veggendosi i Veienti rinchiusi, cominciarono a combattere con tanta rabbia

episodes.description: Vettius Messius, his Volscian army trapped between its occupied stockade and the Roman army, told his soldiers to follow him since not walls but armed men stood against armed men, equal in virtue and superior in necessity — which Livy calls the last and greatest weapon.
episodes.quote: «Ite mecum; non murus nec vallum, armati armatis obstant; virtute pares, quae ultimum ac maximum telum est, necessitate superiores estis»

episodes.description: Camillus, already inside Veii with his army, ordered in the hearing of the Veientes that no one should harm the disarmed, whereupon they threw down their arms and the city was taken almost without blood — a method followed by many captains since.
episodes.quote: comandò, in modo che i Veienti udirono, che nessuno offendessi quegli che fussono disarmati

notes: Livy named explicitly for 'ultimum ac maximum telum' (4.28); the Pontius speech quote matches Livy 9.1.

heading_en: Whether to trust more in a good captain with a weak army or a good army with a weak captain
thesis: Captain and army each need the other, but a good captain with time to instruct and arm his men is more to be trusted than a good army with a tumultuary head, for a good army without a good head becomes insolent and dangerous.
thesis_quote: io credo che sia più da confidare assai in uno capitano che abbi tempo ad instruire uomini e commodità di armargli, che in uno esercito insolente con uno capo tumultuario fatto da lui

propositions.statement: Many good soldiers will more easily find or instruct one man until he becomes a good captain than one man will make many good.
propositions.quote: più facilmente molti buoni troverranno o instruiranno uno, tanto che diventi buono, che non farà uno molti

propositions.statement: A good army without a good head habitually becomes insolent and dangerous.
propositions.quote: uno esercito buono sanza capo buono suole diventare insolente e pericoloso

propositions.statement: Double glory is due to captains who not only had to beat the enemy but had first to instruct their army and make it good.
propositions.quote: è da addoppiare la gloria e la laude a quelli capitani che, non solamente hanno avuto a vincere il nimico, ma, prima che venghino alle mani con quello, è convenuto loro instruire lo esercito loro

episodes.description: Coriolanus, exiled from Rome, raised a Volscian army for revenge and came against Rome, departing more for pity of his mother than for Roman force — the passage where Livy concludes Rome grew more by the virtue of its captains than of its soldiers.
episodes.quote: Essendo diventato Coriolano esule di Roma, se n’andò ai Volsci; dove contratto uno esercito per vendicarsi contro ai suoi cittadini

episodes.description: The Roman army in Spain under the Scipios, after the death of both captains, by its own virtue saved itself, beat the enemy and preserved the province for the republic.
episodes.quote: come occorse nello esercito che i Romani avevano in Ispagna sotto gli Scipioni

episodes.description: Caesar said of Afranius and Petreius in Spain that he went against an army without a leader, and of Pompey in Thessaly that he went against a leader without an army — holding either alone of little account.
episodes.quote: disse che gli stimava poco, «quia ibat ad exercitum sine duce», mostrando la debolezza de’ capitani

episodes.description: Lucullus, wholly inexperienced in war when sent against Mithridates, was quickly made a good captain by his good army full of excellent officers.
episodes.quote: Lucullo, quando fu mandato contro a Mitridate, era al tutto inesperto della guerra

episodes.description: The Romans, for lack of men, armed many slaves and gave them to Sempronius Gracchus to train, who in a short time made a good army of them.
episodes.quote: Armorono i Romani, per difetto di uomini, assai servi, e gli dieno ad esercitare a Sempronio Gracco

episodes.description: Pelopidas and Epaminondas, after freeing Thebes from Spartan servitude, in a short time made excellent soldiers of Theban peasants who could not only withstand the Spartan soldiery but beat it.
episodes.quote: Pelopida ed Epaminonda, come altrove dicemo, poi che gli ebbono tratta Tebe loro patria della servitù degli Spartani

episodes.description: The Macedonian army after Alexander's death, like the veteran soldiers in the Roman civil wars, shows how a good army without a good head becomes insolent and dangerous.
episodes.quote: come diventò lo esercito di Macedonia dopo la morte di Alessandro

notes: Machiavelli explicitly disputes Livy's stated opinion that Rome grew more by captains than soldiers.

heading_en: What effects new inventions appearing in the middle of battle and new voices heard produce
thesis: New sights and new cries arising in the heat of combat can decide battles; a captain should employ such inventions to hearten his own men and dismay the enemy, and be ready to detect and neutralize those of the adversary.
thesis_quote: Di quanto momento sia ne’ conflitti e nelle zuffe uno nuovo accidente che nasca per cosa che di nuovo si vegga o oda

propositions.statement: Popular multitudes are useless for war precisely because every noise, voice or uproar alters them and makes them flee; good orders exist so that small accidents do not disorder the army.
propositions.quote: non per altro le moltitudini popolari sono disutili per la guerra, se non perché ogni romore ogni voce, ogni strepito, gli altera e fagli fuggire

propositions.statement: A good captain must appoint who is to take up his voice and relay it, and accustom his soldiers to believe no one else.
propositions.quote: debbe ordinare chi sono quegli che abbino a pigliare la sua voce e rimetterla ad altri, ed assuefare gli suoi soldati che non credino se non a quelli

propositions.statement: Battlefield deceptions that have more of fiction than of truth should either not be made or be kept at a distance so their weakness is not quickly discovered.
propositions.quote: quando le hanno più del fitto che del vero, è bene, o non le fare o, faccendole, tenerle discosto, di qualità che le non possino essere così presto scoperte

episodes.description: Quinctius, seeing one wing of his army giving way against the Volsci, shouted loudly to stand firm because the other wing was victorious, heartening his men, dismaying the enemy, and winning.
episodes.quote: Quinzio, veggendo inclinare uno de’ corni del suo esercito, cominciò a gridare forte, che gli stessono saldi perché l’altro corno dello esercito era vittorioso

episodes.description: In Perugia the exiled Oddi penetrated the city by night against the Baglioni, but at the last chained street the man breaking the locks, pressed by the crowd, cried 'Fatevi indietro!'; the word 'back!' passed down the ranks and routed the column by itself.
episodes.quote: Era la città di Perugia, pochi anni sono, divisa in due parti, Oddi e Baglioni

episodes.description: The Roman dictator Gaius Sulpicius, giving battle to the Gauls, armed the sutlers and camp rabble, mounted them on mules to look like cavalry behind a hill, and their appearance at a signal at the height of the fight so terrified the Gauls that they lost the battle.
episodes.quote: il quale venendo a giornata con i Franciosi, armò tutti i saccomanni e gente vile del campo

episodes.description: Semiramis, seeing the king of India rich in elephants, made fake ones of buffalo and cow hides on camels to frighten him, but the king discovered the trick and the design turned not only vain but harmful.
episodes.quote: Come fece il re d’India a Semiramis; la quale, veggendo come quel re aveva buono numero di elefanti

episodes.description: The Fidenates sent soldiers out with fire on their lances to dismay the Roman army, but the dictator Mamercus rallied his men, crying shame on fleeing smoke like bees and shouting to destroy Fidenae with its own flames, and the Fidenates' invention failed and they lost the battle.
episodes.quote: «Suis flammis delete Fidenas, quas vestris beneficiis placare non potuistis»

notes: The Latin battle-cry is quoted without naming Livy; chapter-map links it to Livy 4.33.

heading_en: That one and not many should be set over an army, and that several commanders do harm
thesis: Command in war should rest in one man alone: several commanders of equal authority generate confusion and ruin, and it is better to send one man of ordinary prudence than two most able men together with the same authority.
thesis_quote: egli è meglio mandare in una ispedizione uno uomo solo di comunale prudenzia, che due valentissimi uomini insieme con la medesima autorità

propositions.statement: It is most salutary in the administration of great things that supreme command be lodged in one man (Livy's words).
propositions.quote: «Saluberrimum in administratione magnarum rerum est, summam imperii apud unum esse»

propositions.statement: The practice of sending more than one commissioner or head is the principal cause of the ruin of the Italian and French armies of our times.
propositions.quote: E se si cercassi le cagioni della rovina degli eserciti italiani e franciosi ne’ nostri tempi, si troveria la potissima essere stata questa

episodes.description: After the Fidenates rebelled and killed the Roman colony, Rome created four tribunes with consular power and sent three against Fidenae and Veii; divided and disunited, they earned dishonor (though the soldiers' virtue averted real loss), and Rome resorted to creating a dictator so one man might reorder what three had disordered.
episodes.quote: crearono i Romani, per rimediare a questo insulto, quattro Tribuni con potestà consolare

episodes.description: In 1500, when Louis XII's troops were sent to restore Pisa to Florence, the commissioners Giovambatista Ridolfi and Luca degli Albizi shared authority; Luca effaced himself resentfully while Ridolfi was present, but once left alone showed his full worth in spirit, industry and counsel.
episodes.quote: mandò le sue genti a Pisa per ristituirla ai Fiorentini; dove furono mandati commessari Giovambatista Ridolfi e Luca di Antonio degli Albizi

episodes.description: When Quinctius and his colleague Agrippa were sent against the Aequi, Agrippa insisted that the whole administration of the war rest with Quinctius — the occasion of Livy's maxim on sole command.
episodes.quote: essendo mandato da’ Romani contro agli Equi Quinzio ed Agrippa suo collega, Agrippa volle che tutta l’amministrazione della guerra fosse appresso a Quinzio

notes: Two verbatim Livy quotations: 'Tres Tribuni... aperuerunt ad occasionem locum hosti' (4.31) and 'Saluberrimum... apud unum esse' (3.70).

heading_en: True virtue is sought out in difficult times; in easy times, men with wealth or kinship prevail
thesis: In peaceful times great and rare men are neglected out of envy while riches and connections carry men to rank, a disorder that drives slighted citizens to stir trouble; the remedies are to keep citizens poor and to be so ordered for war that reputed citizens are always needed.
thesis_quote: gli uomini grandi e rari in una republica, ne’ tempi pacifichi, sono negletti

propositions.statement: Citizens who see themselves undeservedly despised, and know the easy times are the cause, strive to disturb those times by stirring new wars to the prejudice of the republic.
propositions.quote: quegli cittadini che immeritamente si veggono disprezzare, e conoscono che e’ ne sono cagione i tempi facili e non pericolosi, s’ingegnano di turbargli, movendo nuove guerre in pregiudicio della republica

propositions.statement: The remedies are to keep citizens poor, so wealth without virtue cannot corrupt, and to be ordered for war like early Rome, so reputed citizens are always needed.
propositions.quote: l’uno, mantenere i cittadini poveri, acciocché con le ricchezze sanza virtù e’ non potessino corrompere né loro né altri

episodes.description: In the debate at Athens over the Sicilian expedition reported by Thucydides, Alcibiade and others urged it thinking of their own honor, while Nicias, first among the reputed men, argued against it, saying that in peace many would surpass him but in war none would be his equal.
episodes.quote: Alcibiade e qualche altro cittadino consigliavano che la si facesse, come quelli che, pensando poco al bene publico, pensavono all’onore loro

episodes.description: After Rome had beaten Carthage and Antiochus and no longer feared war, commands went to whoever had popular grace rather than virtue: Paulus Aemilius was repeatedly repulsed for the consulate and only made consul when the dangerous Macedonian war arose and the whole city turned to him.
episodes.quote: Paulo Emilio ebbe più volte la ripulsa nel consolato, né fu prima fatto consolo che surgesse la guerra macedonica

episodes.description: In Florence after 1494 Antonio Giacomini had no competitor while wars were dangerous, but when the siege of Pisa promised honor without risk he was passed over among the three commissioners; the incapable captains dragged out the siege until Florence bought the city it could have taken by force.
episodes.quote: avendosi ad eleggere tre commessari per campeggiare Pisa, e’ fu lasciato indietro

notes: Thucydides cited explicitly for the Athenian example.

heading_en: That a man should not be injured and then sent to an important administration and government
thesis: A republic should take great care not to set over an important administration a citizen to whom a notable injury has been done, for his resentment may lead him to risk or avenge himself upon the state, as Claudius Nero's gamble shows.
thesis_quote: Debbe una republica assai considerare di non preporre alcuno ad alcuna importante amministrazione, al quale sia stato fatto da altri alcuna notabile ingiuria

propositions.statement: If such passions from offenses could do so much in a Roman citizen when Rome was still uncorrupted, one must reckon how much they can do in a citizen of any other, differently made city.
propositions.quote: E quando queste passioni di tali offese possono tanto in uno cittadino romano, e in quegli tempi che Roma ancora era incorrotta, si debbe pensare quanto elle possano in uno cittadino d’un’altra città

propositions.statement: Since no certain remedy exists for such disorders, it is impossible to order a perpetual republic, for its ruin is caused by a thousand unexpected ways.
propositions.quote: gli è impossibile ordinare una republica perpetua, perché per mille inopinate vie si causa la sua rovina

episodes.description: Claudius Nero, dishonored at Rome after Hasdrubal slipped out of his grasp in Spain, as consul left his army facing Hannibal and marched to the Marches to crush Hasdrubal, later admitting he took the gamble that staked Rome's liberty partly to regain his glory and partly to avenge himself on the city that had offended him.
episodes.quote: si partì dallo esercito che lui aveva a fronte ad Annibale, e con parte d’esso ne andò nella Marca, a trovare l’altro Consolo per combattere con Asdrubale

notes: Single-episode chapter; the Metaurus campaign is Livy XXVII, outside Livy I-X.
